checks.claim: Leeuwenhoek was a draper (cloth merchant) in Delft
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Dutch draper from Delft', ran a drapery business selling cloth.

checks.claim: His microscopes had one lens set in a small brass plate
checks.note: Single lens held in a hole between two thin brass plates riveted together, about 5 x 2.5 cm.

checks.claim: Hooke's compound microscope had two lenses in a tube
checks.note: Hooke's instrument had three glasses (objective, removable middle field lens, eye glass); for detailed work he 'took out the middle Glass' and used two. 'Two lenses' is a fair simplification for the detail work; 'two or more lenses' would be fully exact.

checks.claim: Key: the lenses of the day blurred and each extra lens added blur
checks.note: Double-lens microscopes 'suffered from inherent aberrations, both chromatic and, more importantly, spherical'; lensonleeuwenhoek.net/node/7761: 'Three lenses just compounded the aberrations, so two were better'. Grokipedia: compound microscopes 'plagued by chromatic aberration'.

checks.claim: Wrong: a second lens undoes the magnifying of the first
checks.note: False: in a compound microscope the powers multiply (total = ocular x objective).

checks.claim: Wrong: his single lens was much larger
checks.note: False: most surviving lenses are under 3 mm, the best under 1.5 mm.

checks.claim: Wrong: his single lens magnified less
checks.note: False: strongest survivor 266x against about 20-50x for compound microscopes of the day.

checks.claim: Context: Hooke admitted a single lens showed some things more distinctly
checks.note: Hooke, preface to Micrographia (1665): a single lens 'will both magnifie and make some objects more distinct than any of the great Microscopes'. Paraphrase, not quoted: fine.

checks.claim: Context: most lenses under 3 mm; smaller lens magnifies more; best over 250x
checks.note: 'a dozen ... most of them smaller than 3 millimeters'; 'the smaller the lens, the greater the magnification'; strongest surviving instrument 266x (Wikipedia: up to 275x).

checks.claim: Context: Hooke's magnified up to about 50 times
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'magnifications of up to about 50 times' (UCMP gives 20-30x as practical for early compound microscopes; 'up to about 50' is still true).

checks.claim: 1683 letter: white matter between teeth 'about as thick as batter', mixed with pure rain-water
checks.note: Letter of 17 September 1683: 'a little white matter, about as thick as batter'; 'mixed it several times with pure rain-water, in which there were no animalcules' and with saliva; saw 'many very small living animalcules ... which moved very prettily'.

checks.claim: Key: bacteria; letter often called the first clear report of bacteria
checks.note: 'This letter is often cited as the first unambiguous observation of bacteria.' Wikipedia lists bacteria from the human mouth in 1683.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: viruses, mites, algae
checks.note: Viruses are too small for any light lens; mites are arachnids, not what he described; algae are not the organisms of tooth plaque. None defensible.

checks.claim: Context: date 17 September 1683
checks.note: Dated 17 September 1683 (Phil. Trans. misprinted 12 September).

checks.claim: Context: 'his word for such creatures was animalcules, little animals'
checks.note: Leeuwenhoek wrote in Dutch (dierken, diertgens, diertjes, 'little animals'); 'animalcules' is not a Dutch word and was his translator Henry Oldenburg's English rendering (Wikipedia: Oldenburg 'the first to use the word animalcules to translate' the Dutch). Fix: 'his Dutch word for such creatures meant little animals, which his English translators turned into animalcules'.

checks.claim: Context: the rainwater held no animalcules, so they came from his teeth
checks.note: He states the rain-water had no animalcules; the inference is fair.

checks.claim: 1676 letter: more than a million living creatures in one drop of pepper water
checks.note: Letter of 9 October 1676: 'upwards of 1 000 000 living creatures in one drop of pepper-water'.

checks.claim: Some Fellows doubted him
checks.note: 'His credibility was questioned'; observations 'initially met with skepticism'.

checks.claim: Key: a Fellow repeating the observation with his own microscope
checks.note: The Society had Grew, then Hooke, try to repeat it; after Hooke's success the minutes record 'there was no longer any doubt of Mr. LEEWENHOECK'S discovery'.

checks.claim: Wrong: eight respected men of Delft vouching
checks.note: He did send 'eight testimonies from gentlemen of repute' (a minister, a notary, a barrister...), none natural philosophers; testimony is weaker than independent repetition. Real but not strongest: fine as a wrong choice.

checks.claim: Wrong: his drawings; a longer letter counting drop by drop
checks.note: Both still depend on Leeuwenhoek alone; Oldenburg asked for his method 'that others may confirm such Observations'.

checks.claim: Context: he would not explain his methods
checks.note: 'Leeuwenhoek declined to describe his methods throughout his life'; Wikipedia: parts he 'only keep for myself'.

checks.claim: Context: Society asked Hooke; November 1677, after two failures, Hooke saw 'great numbers of exceedingly small animals swimming to and fro' before Wren and others
checks.note: Asked in October 1677; failed 1 and 8 November; succeeded 15 November 1677 (Lane 2015: 'third attempt'); witnesses named in the minutes include Wren, Grew, Hoskyns, Aubrey. Quote is from the minutes (Birch).

checks.claim: Context: minutes record no longer any doubt
checks.note: 'there was no longer any doubt of Mr. LEEWENHOECK'S discovery'.

checks.claim: Plant cells easy to see because of thick walls; animal cells have no wall
checks.note: OpenStax: plant cells 'relatively easy' to see, 'clearly separated by their thick cell walls'.

checks.claim: Schleiden argued in 1838 that every plant is built of cells
checks.note: 1838, 'Contributions to Phytogenesis': all plant tissues consist of cells.

checks.claim: Schwann showed in 1839 that animals are built of cells
checks.note: Mikroskopische Untersuchungen (1839): animal tissues 'composed of cells, each of which has a nucleus'.

checks.claim: Key: he looked for the nucleus
checks.note: Williams, A History of Science: Schwann reasoned 'the nucleus should also be found in the ultimate particles of animal tissues', and found nuclei in abundance, especially in embryonic tissue. Wikipedia and Hektoen agree the nucleus was the link.

checks.claim: Context: Schleiden held the nucleus most important; talk of nuclei; Schwann remembered similar structures in animal cells
checks.note: 'their conversation turned on the nuclei of plant and animal cells'; Schwann recalled similar structures in notochord cells. The dinner's date and setting vary (1837 or 1838) but the draft uses only the talk of nuclei, which all accounts share.

checks.claim: Wrong: chloroplasts, central vacuole (animal cells have neither)
checks.note: Animal cells lack chloroplasts and the large central vacuole of plant cells.

checks.claim: Wrong: mitochondria, not described until 1857
checks.note: Kölliker 'first described these organelles as small granules in the muscle cells of insects' in 1857; named by Benda 1898.

checks.claim: Remak observed dividing red blood cells of chicken embryos and frog eggs
checks.note: 'observing red blood cells from chicken embryos in various stages of division'; confirmed it 'in the cell of every frog's egg immediately after fertilization'.

checks.claim: In 1852 he published what he saw
checks.note: 1852: 'convincing evidence that cells are derived from other cells as a result of cell division' (Ueber extracellulare Entstehung thierischer Zellen und ueber Vermehrung derselben durch Theilung). Minor: his first blood-cell paper was 1841 (zientzia.eus; Garrison-Morton), and the frog-egg work came out in 1852, so 'by 1852' would be the more exact wording. Not wrong as written.

checks.claim: Virchow made the idea famous three years later (1855) in four Latin words, without naming Remak
checks.note: Omnis cellula e cellula, published 1855 (Embryo Project, Grokipedia). Britannica and Wikipedia note the epigram was coined by Raspail (1825) and popularized by Virchow; the stem says 'made the idea famous', which stays true.

checks.claim: Key: splitting in two to make new cells
checks.note: Cell division, as above.

checks.claim: Wrong: forming out of the surrounding fluid; growing larger; forming from specks in the blood
checks.note: Fluid/crystal formation was Schleiden's and Schwann's mistaken idea, the opposite of Remak's; the other two are not what he reported.

checks.claim: Context: against Schleiden's and Schwann's idea that cells form out of a fluid, as crystals do; his work went largely unnoticed
checks.note: OpenStax: Schleiden 'believed that cells formed through crystallization'; Wikipedia: Schwann 'hypothesized that living cells formed in ways similar to the formation of crystals'; Embryo Project: Remak's 'publication went largely unnoticed'.

checks.claim: Context: Virchow at first doubted cell division
checks.note: 'did not initially accept the evidence for cell division'; Grokipedia: 'initially resisted the idea of direct division'.

checks.claim: Context: his essay never mentioned Remak; Weindling calls it plagiarism
checks.note: OpenStax: Virchow 'neglected to credit Remak's ideas in his essay' and by today's standards it 'would certainly be considered an act of plagiarism'; zientzia.eus: Virchow 'did not even mention Remak'; Wikipedia (Remak): per Paul Weindling, Virchow 'plagiarized Remak's notion'. Attributed to a named historian, so told fairly.

checks.claim: Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built the electron microscope in Berlin in 1931
checks.note: First prototype transmission electron microscope, Technical University of Berlin (Technische Hochschule Charlottenburg), 1931.

checks.claim: It uses a beam of electrons and shows far finer detail than any light microscope
checks.note: True of the kind (0.1 nm against about 200 nm). Note: the 1931 prototype itself did not yet beat the light microscope; Wikipedia: 'In the following year, 1933, Ruska and Knoll built the first electron microscope that exceeded the resolution of an optical (light) microscope'. The stem's present tense describes the kind, so it stands; if the writer wants it airtight, 'Within two years, such microscopes showed far finer detail...'.

checks.claim: Key: viruses, most too small for any light microscope
checks.note: 'Most virus species have virions too small to be seen with an optical microscope'; 'most of them' rightly hedges for the few large viruses.

checks.claim: Wrong: bacteria, cell nuclei, chloroplasts
checks.note: Bacteria visible at about 400x; nucleus named by Robert Brown 1831 with a light microscope; chloroplasts visible as green ovals under a light microscope (Grokipedia Chloroplast).

checks.claim: Context: first pictures of tobacco mosaic virus by electron microscope in 1939
checks.note: Kausche, Pfankuch and Helmut Ruska, 1939, 'the first images of the virus' (Naturwissenschaften 27:292-299). The context claims only the first TMV images, not the first virus ever imaged: correct.

checks.claim: Context: most viruses about a hundredth the size of a bacterium
checks.note: About one-hundredth the size of most bacteria.

checks.claim: Context: Leeuwenhoek saw bacteria more than 250 years earlier
checks.note: 1683 to 1939 is 256 years (the sentence before names 1939).

checks.claim: Key: the diaphragm controls the light; closing it cuts glare and a washed-out look
checks.note: Carolina: diaphragm 'located just under the stage'; 'Decreasing the aperture of the diaphragm will reduce glare and increase contrast'. AmScope: 'Too much light tends to give the specimen a washed-out appearance.' OpenStax: light adjusted 'by opening or closing a diaphragm'.

checks.claim: Wrong: fine focus knob, eyepiece lens, stage clips
checks.note: Fine focus moves for small focusing changes; the eyepiece magnifies; clips hold the slide. None controls the light.

checks.claim: Key: the coarse knob could crash the high-power lens into the slide
checks.note: AmScope: high-power objectives are very close to the slide and 'using the coarse focus knob can scratch the lens and crack the slide'. Carolina: 'Never use the coarse-focus adjustment at high power. That can damage both the slide and the objective.'

checks.claim: Coarse knob for low power, fine knob for high power
checks.note: Coarse for 'large-scale movements with 4x and 10x'; fine for 'small-scale movements, especially with 40x or 100x'.

checks.claim: Wrong: changes the power; moves the slide side to side; dims the light
checks.note: Coarse knob 'moves the stage or body tube up and down'; it neither changes magnification (the objective does), moves the slide sideways (stage controls), nor dims the light (diaphragm).

checks.claim: Key: total magnification = eyepiece x objective (10 x 40 = 400)
checks.note: 'The total magnification is the product of the ocular magnification times the objective magnification'; Grokipedia Optical microscope gives 10x x 40x = 400x.

checks.claim: Eyepiece 10x; high-power objective 40x just above the slide
checks.note: Oculars 'typically magnify images 10 times'; objectives 4x to 100x.

checks.claim: Wrong: add (50); objective alone; eyepiece alone
checks.note: All false given the product rule.

checks.claim: Context: 400x is enough to make out bacteria
checks.note: 'bacteria, which are visible at about 400x or so'.

unit_notes: One error, in a context line: Leeuwenhoek did not use the word animalcules himself (he wrote Dutch dierkens/diertgens; Oldenburg's English translation made 'animalcules'). Minor wording notes, not errors: Hooke's microscope had three lenses with a removable middle one (two used for detail work); Remak's chick blood-cell paper was 1841 and his division paper 1852; the 1931 electron microscope prototype first beat light resolution in 1933; 'omnis cellula e cellula' was coined by Raspail (1825), popularized by Virchow (the draft says only that Virchow made it famous). Not re-checked: The Scientist's dinner date, which the draft does not use.
